Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words from two worlds. Crumb is the inside of the loaf, the part bakers obsess over. Code is the structure that holds modern things together. The brand sits between hand work and rigor.
Modern.industrySummary: Sourdough went mainstream during the pandemic. Now every neighborhood has a bakery that calls itself craft. The market is asking for the next step. Something that respects the bread but doesn't worship it.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Tartine (tartinebakery.com) is the canon. Sullivan Street Bakery (sullivanstreetbakery.com) sells the volume. She Wolf Bakery (shewolfbakery.com) does the Brooklyn version. Most lean rustic. We lean modern.
Modern.positioningStatement: A bakery for people who care about the bread and don't need the wood-and-flour story.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Eats out three nights a week. Cooks the other four. Knows which bakery a chef uses. Will drive across town for a good loaf. Doesn't need the loaf wrapped in butcher paper to know it's good.

dos: Update the menu like a software changelog
donts: Photograph the baker with flour on his face

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark in a precise grotesk, with the ampersand styled as a tight braid or twist. A second mark, a clean cross-section of a loaf in line art, used as the app icon and on the take-home box stamp.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for ingredient lists and pricing
typography.rationale: One typeface family. The mono is for facts. The regular is for the brand. Two voices, one shelf.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No flour-on-the-apron photography. No founder origin story on the bag. No Friday market van with wooden crates.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A clean shop with a glass case, a board listing today's three breads, and one chalkboard with tomorrow's pastry list. Web ordering opens at 5 a.m. and closes when the day's loaves are claimed.

Luxury.tagline: Bread, since attention was a virtue.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: Maison sets the register. A house, not a shop. Lebrun is a baker's name from another century. Together it reads as a small French institution. The accent on the brand is on patience.
Luxury.story: Maison Lebrun began as a single oven in a stone room. We grew slowly, by intention. We still make the same number of loaves a day as the day we opened. Some people wait. Most do.
Luxury.industrySummary: There's a luxury food market that has run out of objects to elevate. Chocolate, salt, olive oil, even ice cubes. Bread sits there still. Plain on the counter. We think that's the opportunity.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Poilâne (poilane.com) wrote the playbook. Du Pain et des Idées (dupainetdesidees.com) holds the Parisian charm. Tartine (tartinebakery.com) goes American luxury. We are quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The bread house for people who treat bread the way other people treat wine.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 70. Wealthy. Has a chef at home or knows the chef at the restaurant. Eats bread the way it was meant to be eaten, with salted butter and silence. Will pay twelve dollars for the right loaf.

dos: Use accurate French where it fits
Name the flour, the mill, and the miller

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark with a small wheat sheaf used as a hallmark, not a logo. The sheaf goes on wax paper, on the back of the price tag, on the door handle. The wordmark goes on the awning, the box, the bag.

typography.secondary: Söhne for the menu and operational signage
typography.rationale: A classical serif sets the heritage tone. A modern grotesk handles the legibility for the menu and the website.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No franchise. No second location for now. No grocery store distribution. No collabs. No app.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: The definite article in front of the most basic word for the thing. We don't name the brand after the maker. We name it after the product. Honest and quiet.
Minimal.industrySummary: There are too many bakery brands. Every one of them has a story, a logo, a sourdough origin tale. Most of them are good. Almost none of them are quiet.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Tartine, Du Pain et des Idées, every neighborhood Brooklyn bakery. The reference shelf is full. The shelf for quiet is empty.
Minimal.positioningStatement: The bakery that doesn't make a fuss about being a bakery.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who buy bread once or twice a week and don't need a story to go with it. They have a regular order. They don't want to talk.

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. THE LOAF set in a single weight grotesk, all caps, wide spacing. No icon. The bag has the wordmark and the price. The receipt has the date.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No bag art. No founder story. No social campaigns. No paper price tags written by hand. Plain printing, plain paper.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Wheat names the product. Order names the discipline. Company closes it like a business. The whole thing sounds like it has been around since the 1940s, even if it's two years old.
Corporate.industrySummary: Restaurants and grocers spend more than they should on bread because the supplier is unreliable. The category is dominated by either huge factory bakers or precious craft bakeries that can't scale. Few players sit in the middle.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Aryzta (aryzta.com) is the industrial giant. Boudin (boudinbakery.com) handles the West Coast wholesale. La Brea Bakery (labreabakery.com) is the premium wholesale standard. We are smaller, faster, more direct.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Wholesale bread that arrives at six, every day, and tastes like it was baked in a real oven.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Restaurant operations live and die on delivery reliability. We compete on showing up first, with bread that the head chef approves the first time.

targetAudience.primary: Restaurant owners, head chefs, grocer buyers, hotel F&B managers. They sign weekly purchase orders. They have a short list of bakers they trust.
motivations: Bread that doesn't change between deliveries

dos: Speak to the buyer, not the diner

messagingPillars.name: On time, every time

messagingPillars.name: The same bread, every time
messagingPillars.description: Standardized recipes, calibrated ovens, single mill source. No batch variation.

messagingPillars.name: One contact, one invoice
messagingPillars.description: One account manager per restaurant. One invoice per month.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No retail shop. No D2C. No specialty croissants. No seasonal limited editions. Bread, on time, at scale.

Creative.tagline: Membership has its perks. Also: cookies.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Crust is the most flavorful part. Club implies you belong. The pair sounds like a place that throws a good party. The name lives on a hoodie before it lives on a sign.
Creative.manifesto: We started Crust Club because we wanted a bakery that felt like a place to hang out. Not a museum. Not a temple. Not a TikTok set. A real bakery with a sticky door handle and a sticker wall and bread that ruins other bread for you.
Creative.industrySummary: Bakeries got serious. The serious ones are great but they're not fun. There's room for one that has personality, throws events, sells T-shirts, and still makes really good bread.
Creative.competitorLandscape: She Wolf Bakery (shewolfbakery.com) is Brooklyn earnest. Bub and Grandma's (bubandgrandmas.com) has the LA charm. Levain (levainbakery.com) figured out the line-out-the-door bakery. We're more clubhouse than counter.
Creative.positioningStatement: The bakery that throws the party and makes the bread.

targetAudience.primary: 20s and 30s. Lives in a city. Has a friend group they post photos with. Joins things. Wears the merch. Buys a loaf and a totebag in the same trip.
